business_problem: General Motors wanted to improve safety, quality, ergonomics, planning speed, and operational efficiency across its global manufacturing footprint while reducing downtime in highly competitive vehicle production.
solution_summary: GM describes an in-house AI implementation embedded across its global manufacturing network rather than a single off-the-shelf platform. Before new lines are built, the company uses digital twins to simulate a running production line so planners can test configurations, identify issues early, and speed factory scaling while saving time and money. On operating production assets, AI and machine-learning techniques are used to detect potential battery-pack leaks quickly and accurately, enabling rapid repair and supporting battery safety and quality. GM also combines robotics with a proprietary AI tool at inspection stages to examine welds and paint coats for irregularities and anomalies. These capabilities feed manufacturing, quality, repair, safety, and ergonomics workflows inside plants to reduce downtime, improve worker conditions, and raise vehicle quality. The article does not name storage platforms or third-party infrastructure, but it makes clear the solutions are built in-house and tightly integrated into planning and shop-floor operations.

data_flow: Production-line designs are modeled in digital twins before construction, while live manufacturing inputs from battery packs, welds, and paint coats are analyzed by GM's AI, machine-learning, robotics, and proprietary inspection tools. The resulting defect, anomaly, and planning insights are used by planners, repair teams, quality teams, and plant staff to fix issues quickly, reduce downtime, and improve safety and quality.
